stem: The contract’s credit arrangement most directly explains why sharecroppers

options.text: quickly saved enough to buy their own farms
options.misconception: Credit at the store helped workers save and buy land.

options.text: moved freely between plantations each season
options.misconception: Sharecroppers could leave whenever they wished.

options.text: ended most years deeper in debt to the landowner
refused to grow cotton and planted food crops instead

rationales.A: Credit at the landowner’s store drained earnings; it did not build savings.
rationales.B: Background: debt tied the cropper to the land, since leaving meant abandoning the crop that secured the debt.
rationales.C: The landowner advances the supplies, keeps the accounts, and takes his payment from the crop first. Background: When the crop fell short, the unpaid balance carried over, so the debt grew year after year.
rationales.D: Background: the landowner decided the crop, and cotton was what the market and the debt demanded.
rationales.general:
1. Trace the money. The landowner lends the supplies and keeps the books.
2. Ask who gets paid first. The landowner takes his share after the debts are settled.
3. Ask what happens in a bad year. Background: The unpaid debt carries over, so the balance grows.
4. Match the outcome. Background: A worker who owes more each year cannot save, leave, or choose his crop.
Remember: when one side lends the supplies and keeps the accounts, the debt is the leash.

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrased from sharecropping contracts of the period, including the De Soto County, Mississippi, contract of 1867 (Salisbury University, Nabb Research Center). Image: title page of the 1867 De Soto County contract.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of a sharecropping contract, De Soto County, Mississippi, 1867. The freedmen agree to work the landowner’s plantation for one year. The landowner furnishes the land, seed, tools, and housing. The freedmen receive one-half of the crop after the debts for supplies are paid. Supplies are bought on credit from the landowner, and the crop stands as security for the debt.

source: original; stimulus paraphrases sharecropping contracts of the period, with the title page of the 1867 De Soto County contract
